paper_title: Shuffles of Context-Free Languages Along Regular Trajectories
classifications: Theory of computation → Grammars and context-free languages
statement: We have examined the conditions under which shuffling two nonregular CFL along a regular trajectory results in another CFL. In doing so, we investigated the notion of couplings, i.e., portions of words where a PDA has to push and pop respectively. We demonstrated that these couplings must exist (Coupling Lemmas), that they can survive being shuffled (Resilience Lemmas), and applied these tools to the study of trajectories of shuffles. There, we demonstrate that some trajectories never shuffle two nonCFLs into CFLs, and further characterized the behavior of said trajectories with respect to shuffling DCFLs. The most pressing question left open by this work is to extend this latter characterization to CFLs. Bérard [2] hints at the fact that this will be much harder: Indeed, (st)∗ (s∗ + t∗ ) can shuffle some nonregular CFLs into a CFL, and it is not known if the same holds for (s∗ + t∗ )(st)∗ (s∗ + t∗ ). We do not venture to conjecture one way or another. Similarly, this question is mirrored in the general coupling lemma: does there exist a stronger description of when couplings do (or do not) exist in the general case?
context: 7 Conclusion and Perspectives We have examined the conditions under which shuffling two nonregular CFL along a regular trajectory results in another CFL. In doing so, we investigated the notion of couplings, i.e., portions of words where a PDA has to push and pop respectively. We demonstrated that these couplings must exist (Coupling Lemmas), that they can survive being shuffled (Resilience Lemmas), and applied these tools to the study of trajectories of shuffles. There, we demonstrate that some trajectories never shuffle two nonCFLs into CFLs, and further characterized the behavior of said trajectories with respect to shuffling DCFLs. The most pressing question left open by this work is to extend this latter characterization to CFLs. Bérard [2] hints at the fact that this will be much harder: Indeed, (st)∗ (s∗ + t∗ ) can shuffle some nonregular CFLs into a CFL, and it is not known if the same holds for (s∗ + t∗ )(st)∗ (s∗ + t∗ ). We do not venture to conjecture one way or another. Similarly, this question is mirrored in the general coupling lemma: does there exist a stronger description of when couplings do (or do not) exist in the general case? Going further than shuffles along regular trajectories, one could study context-free trajectories, an avenue of research started by Mateescu et al. [10]. Further, (trajectory-based) variants of the so-called synchronized shuffle [20], in which some letters act as synchronizations, ought to be studied in the same way, in particular given their relevance in molecular biology. (See also [19] for an extensive list of references pertaining to this shuffle.)
